title: No 'surprise' about Sabah's progress
description: Journalist Katie Wilson, who covers football in Azerbaijan, joined BBC Radio Manchester's Michael Clarke and Wes Brown on Total Sport to give an insight into Thursday's Champions League opponents Sabah.  Wilson said the club's progress should not come as a surprise, despite their relative lack of experience.  "The club is only nine years old, they had to go through four qualifying rounds," she explained.
fullText:
Journalist Katie Wilson, who covers football in Azerbaijan, joined BBC Radio Manchester's Michael Clarke and Wes Brown on Total Sport to give an insight into Thursday's Champions League opponents Sabah.

Wilson said the club's progress should not come as a surprise, despite their relative lack of experience.

"The club is only nine years old, they had to go through four qualifying rounds," she explained.

"I think in Azerbaijan it's not such a surprise, this was always the intention when the club was launched. It was always the intention to compete in Europe."

Asked whether there would be a big gulf in quality, Wilson said Sabah would be determined to make an impact after navigating four qualifying rounds.

"You don't go through four qualifying rounds to just be happy to be there. I think they really will want to get some points. I think being from a smaller association where people don't know too much about them could actually be an opportunity to make the most of that.

"People won't know their style, and if we look at how they fared in the qualifying rounds, sometimes they went in as the underdog but were able to overturn it.

"Maybe if United have control of the game and get comfortable, that's when Sabah could be quite dangerous."

Wilson also revealed an unusual detail about Sabah manager Valdas Dambrauskas, who funded his coaching education after appearing on a TV gameshow.

She explained: "Dambrauskas didn't have a professional playing career but he did go on 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?' in Lithuania when he was 25-years-old, I believe. He won 4,000 litas, which is around £1,000. He used that to fund his coaching course in the UK."

title: 'Spoke brilliantly' but Liverpool fans torn on Mac Allister contract comments
description: Alexis Mac Allister splits opinion on his public comments regarding his contract at Liverpool, as fans and BBC Sport pundit Pat Nevin share opinions.
fullText:
Did Alexis Mac Allister strike the right tone when he told the media about his contract situation with Liverpool?

The Argentine midfielder has a deal with the Reds until 2028, but said on Tuesday that he is "very sad" not to have received a new contract in the summer after team-mates Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch penned new agreements.

The public approach to stalling contract dealings is nothing new at Liverpool.

In November 2024, Mohamed Salah spoke openly about his contract stalemate when he admitted he was "disappointed" by a lack of offers from the club, as he entered the final six months of his deal.

Salah was eventually offered an extension and Mac Allister will be hoping for the same.

But as they were with Salah, opinions are split on whether taking it public was the fair thing to do.

Fans contacting BBC Sport claim the ordeal is "self-indulgent", while former Everton and Chelsea winger, Pat Nevin believes Mac Allister "said exactly the right things".

Nevin told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast: "I often hear various players saying things and pushing things a certain way and you get a bit fed up with it.

"You're thinking, 'go whinge and whine somewhere else mate, you're doing OK'. Not this time.

"I thought he spoke brilliantly. I thought he said exactly the right things - that he loves the club. Any fan watching that is thinking how he just wants to play for Liverpool Football Club.

"He's just shown us that is the case and if you are asked the question you answer it honestly. He is saying he's seen his mates getting these contracts which might be disappointing, but he's saying all the correct things I think.

"I take nothing away from that, I applaud him for all that.

"Things can change very quickly. It didn't look like Cody Gakpo would leave very recently and then suddenly he's knocking.

"If he is asking for far too much money and putting that pressure on it then he is playing a very good game because to speak the way he did there didn't sound like that. It sounded like somebody who just wanted a contract offered."

BBC Radio Merseyside also discussed the situation with Liverpool fan, Joel Richards, who called Mac Allister's comments a "clever tactic".

"Mac Allister's at an age now, 27, where his next contract is going to be the biggest one of his career," Richards said.

"He is someone who will be looking to be remunerated properly after seeing his team-mates getting bumper pay rises so, of course he's going to put it out there that he came very close to leaving in the summer.

"I'd say it's a clever tactic but how many times have we been here with footballers when they get a microphone put in front of them? If it wasn't going to happen here before a Champions League game, it would have happened with Argentina on international duty.

"Objectively speaking, if you're going to canvas the opinions of a decent size of Liverpool fans from last season, asked them what you thought on Mac Allister and whether he was deserving of a new deal, I think a large majority of that sample size would say 'no' simply because of the performances that he put in.

"However, it's easy to focus on the negatives of last season whereas, his first two seasons at Liverpool he was an important player for us."

Liverpool's communications department have dealt with tricky player-led controversies in recent times.

Salah told media he had been "thrown under the bus" during a stand-off with former boss Arne Slot last season, Dominik Szoboszlai had to clear up a move to shrug his shoulders at fans after defeat at Manchester City and now Mac Allister has made contract frustration public.

Some fans think the World Cup winner could have held back.

Writing in to BBC Sport, supporter Rob said Mac Allister "should do his talking on the pitch, not off it", while fan Patricio said the move was "childish" and that the midfielder should "earn" an extension.

BBC Sport reader David wrote: "Very poor from Mac Allister on so many levels. He still has two years remaining on his existing contract, had a very poor season so is not in a position to renegotiate terms unlike other players he referred to, and no doubt he is fully aware there will be a time to negotiate a new contract later in the season if his form improves."

And fan Stuart added: "Self-indulgent and not in any way helpful. Alexis was there to represent the club ahead of a huge match and first major Anfield occasion for Iraola, not to air his contract grievance. You're not bigger than the club even if you are a World Cup winner."

title: Which NFL team should you support?
description: As the NFL returns for a new season, BBC Sport helps you choose your ideal team to follow.
fullText:
Some 213 days after the Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots at Super Bowl 60, the NFL returns, with the same sides meeting again to open the season.

On Wednesday (01:20 BST, Thursday) the Patriots travel to Lumen Field to play a Seahawks team hoping to become only the ninth franchise to win the title in consecutive seasons.

If you're in the market for a team to follow this year, BBC Sport is here to help.

We've crunched the numbers on a wide range of categories to put the information at your fingertips - and there's a handy quiz at the end to help you figure out your best fit.

Let's start with the top dogs - the trophy winners.

Leading the way with six Super Bowls each are the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Patriots, the latter all coming since the turn of the century under legendary coach Bill Belichick.

Not far behind are the Dallas Cowboys, known as 'America's team', and the San Francisco 49ers, who have each won five.

Taking in the pre-Super Bowl era, the Green Bay Packers have the most NFL championships with 13, including four Super Bowl wins.

At the other end of the spectrum, 12 franchises have never won the Vince Lombardi Trophy, including the Buffalo Bills and the Minnesota Vikings, who have both lost four times in the Super Bowl.

Perhaps silverware isn't everything to you.

If history is more your bag, four teams have been around for 100 years or more. The Arizona Cardinals, Chicago Bears, New York Giants and Green Bay Packers were all established in the 1920s.

For those who prefer more modern upstarts, look no further than the Houston Texans, who only started competing in the NFL in 2002.

We took a calculation of the centre of the UK being a location in Lancashire and figured out the distance from that point to each franchise's stadium in the US.

East Coast teams such as the New England Patriots, Philadelphia Eagles and the two New York teams - the Giants and Jets - are the closest by that metric, coming in at just over 3,000 miles away.

If you would prefer to get as far away from home as possible, shoot across the US towards the Pacific Ocean and opt for the Los Angeles Chargers or Rams, fully 5,263 miles away as the crow flies.

Any NFL game is a major event and, as amply demonstrated during the football World Cup this summer, the US is full of stadiums to suit.

We took the average attendance for each team over the past five seasons to calculate the biggest - and it was the AT&T Stadium in Dallas, where England played their opening group game against Croatia.

The lowest average was the Chicago Bears, with element-exposed Soldier Field the only stadium to come in under 60,000.

The franchise are developing plans for a venue across the state border in Hammond, Indiana.

Taking US weather data from 1991 to 2020, we looked at the range of temperatures from highest to lowest across all 32 areas.

It is no surprise that the hottest areas will affect desert teams Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, with Florida's Miami Dolphins and Tampa Bay Buccaneers also offering scorching summers and mild winters.

If that is not for you, then 12 franchises have an average lowest temperature under freezing, including the Vikings, whose average in January is -8C.

Since first jetting to London in 2013, the Jacksonville Jaguars have played in the UK 14 times, and will stretch that further when they play back-to-back weeks there in October.

That number far outstrips every other franchise, with the Buffalo Bills playing six times in the now defunct Toronto Series of the mid-2000s and twice in London, and the Miami Dolphins third with seven overseas games.

The NFL continues to extend its reach with nine international games planned for 2026, including a maiden trip to Australia when the San Francisco 49ers face the LA Rams at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on opening weekend.

The Dallas Cowboys, whose only previous appearance on foreign soil was in 2014 at Wembley against the Jaguars, will play the Baltimore Ravens at another iconic world stadium, the Maracana in Rio de Janeiro, at the end of September.

title: McLaren talks, 'numb' cars and being 'captain of the ship' - Verstappen Q&A
description: In an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, Max Verstappen talks about his new contract at Red Bull and much more.
fullText:
Max Verstappen is in a no-nonsense mood - even more than usual.

The Red Bull driver is renowned for his straight talking but now, as he discusses his 2026 season so far in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, he is at his most uncompromising.

We're talking on the eve of last weekend's Italian Grand Prix. The temperature is into the mid-30Cs, Red Bull's hospitality unit is not coping well, and Verstappen's PR handler messages before the Dutchman turns up to suggest I find a table near a fan; the interview might be more positive that way.

Monza is the second race since the four-time world champion signed a two-year contract extension with Red Bull.

In theory, this runs to the end of 2030. In reality, it changes little. It still has performance clauses. So Verstappen is earning a bit more money but, if Red Bull are still struggling for competitiveness next year, there will remain the prospect he could look for pastures new.

Verstappen arrives and briefly adjusts the fan blowing in our direction. "It's too hot in here," he says.

Does he need a breather before we start? "No, no," he says. "I'm good. It was just that it was super-hot in the corner when I was doing the print [media]."

Verstappen is always a great interviewee. Direct, honest, uncompromising.

Now, for whatever reason, he is especially frank and open, as we discuss why he extended his contract, his discussions with McLaren, his stunning appearance at the Nurburgring 24 Hours in May, and the new Formula 1 engine rules, with which it is no secret he has a problem.

Where's your head at, Max, in terms of how the season has gone so far?

"Of course it's not where I want to be, but as a team we're trying to just learn and understand a lot of things for next year. We are not in a title fight. We are just trying to find more performance.

"Changes need to happen to the car for next year. We will not be able to change that for this year, but we just need to try and get a lot of learnings to do better next year."

"Overall we're just lacking a bit of performance. The car is not where I want it to be feeling-wise, and the through-corner balance is too hit and miss between entry, mid and exit.

"It's just fundamentally something in the car that we need to try and work on for the next year."

This has been a bit of a theme for longer than this year. How concerning is it that that's happening across a different set of regulations?

"That's exactly that. There's also things that we talk about within the team, like how can that happen, how can we fix it? That's basically what we are doing now and trying to do now.

"Some people have left, new people have come in. With the new people, we are discussing what we can do about it. Is that just some changes, a different philosophy? All these kind of things."

What made you sign a new contract?

"It comes down to also feeling well within a team. This is like a second family to me.

"The belief that you can turn things around, you can build towards hopefully a better future with other people, new people. And at the end of the day, it's not only Formula 1 for me. There are a lot of things that I'm doing next year that Red Bull is involved in as well.

"I feel good here. So this, for me, is the right place to be."

Did it take much for them to convince you to do it?

"I always said to them: 'Don't stress about it, just work on the car.' Because the faster the car goes, the easier the decision is anyway.

"I can understand, of course, maybe sometimes they were a little bit worried. But at the same time, for me, I was just worried about here, what was going on.

"At the same time, I was very busy with my stuff also outside of Formula 1. So I never really spent a lot of time talking or doing different things or trying to go somewhere else."

From the outside, it's hard to see what they could have done to convince you things will improve.

"I don't mind the challenge also. I don't have that desire or need to show in another car that I can win it, or whatever.

"It's easy to run to the fastest car and then do it all again. But it's not how I am. You cannot be the captain of the ship and as soon as there is something not working, you jump off the ship.

"It's been a bit downwards from the dominant years, but I don't mind also rebuilding it. It's another challenge as well."

You talked to Mercedes last year, McLaren this year. How serious was that?

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously. They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice. You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

What race have you enjoyed most this year?

"Probably the Nordschleife [Nurburgring 24 Hours]. It was super-cool to be able to do an endurance event with my team-mates, the guys that won with the car throughout the main season.

"We knew that we were going to be really strong. We peaked at the right time, but unfortunately the car retired. It was an incredible experience. And pure. Pure motorsport."

Your first stint, where you went from 10th to first, was so impressive.

"I was enjoying it. Not easy conditions. It started to drizzle. The track was slippery. Crashes. Code 60s [when a stretch of track is limited to 60km/h after an incident].

"Some people were like: 'Let's see how he will do in the race under pressure with all these kinds of scenarios that he has never done before.'

"But I have done them a million times on the simulator. I have done so many laps and 24-hour races on the simulator. I never felt out of depth or whatever. I was fully zoned in. I just had a great time.

"Once I was in the race, you switch to another level. I was just in a zone. It's really enjoyable."

You want to go back to Nurburgring to win that race. Is there anything else on your bucket list?

"All the endurance races. Eventually, of course also Hypercar [the world endurance championship]. I don't want to rush it. I want to do it in the right environment. On my terms. And competitive."

Is it true you want to do Le Mans with Fernando Alonso?

"We've talked about it. I mean, look at Fernando. He's 45 and he's still flying. Especially for Le Mans, with his experience, it could be a good option. It needs to fit our schedules. It needs to make sense. It needs to be on my terms. And there needs to be a real chance to go there and win it."

You have been clear about your distaste for the new F1 engine rules this year and at the Japanese Grand Prix you said: 'Is it worth it?' What convinced you it was?

"Hoping that it will be better in the future. Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

So that people can understand why the drivers have been upset this year, what is it about these hybrid engines, and the need to recharge the batteries, that detracts from the best drivers' abilities?

"In the history of the sport, normally the driver that is the most committed, the latest on the brakes, earlier on throttle, committing in the high speed, they get rewarded, because you just gain that time in the corner.

"But now you're constantly thinking about, 'In this corner I might have to hold in a bit. Go later on throttle. Or brake earlier. Or lift off. And then I have more top speed.' Stuff like that. It's so unnatural. It's so not how it should be.

"No disrespect. And I hope no-one picks up on this. But look at Yuki [Tsunoda]. He jumps in the [Racing Bulls] car [at the Dutch Grand Prix]. Never driven the car before. Immediately competitive.

"Liam [Lawson] jumps from the Racing Bulls to the Red Bull - immediately competitive. It's because these cars are numb to your driver inputs.

"Of course, yes, you still have to do a good lap. And you still have to commit. The fastest drivers will always come out on top. But it's really, really limited, like a choke hold or something. You're held back."

Formula 1 as a sport has accepted that it needs to change, and the internal combustion-electrical split is changing to 60-40 in two steps by 2028. But what would you like to see for the new engine formula 1 in 2030 or 2031?

"It has to go back to a V8, just for drivability already. When you drive the old cars, you cannot imagine the difference in how the engine responds, or the drivability you get. And how terrible or horrible it actually is now compared to just having a V8."

What about compared to last year's turbo-hybrid engines?

"Also horrible, the feeling compared to a V8. The V8 is so much better. It is so much more free, lighter. Cars are so heavy nowadays.

"It is better to just have a smaller V8 engine, much lighter. Try to really limit the battery size to maybe like a kind of push-to-pass battery. But you should not have it involved or any kind of proper normal performance running."

And you would have no turbo either?

"Ideally not, because that introduces turbo lag."

So what do you enjoy about F1 these days? The competition and prestige more than the actual purity of the racing?

"I have been lucky that the years before have been quite decent [in terms of results]. Not how I wanted it to be with the battery side of things.

"But just the emotion of the V8, of the V10, back in the day, when I was a kid. You walk around, you hear these cars go out, you have goosebumps.

"Even if you go 300km/h compared to now sometimes 350, 360, it doesn't matter.

"It is the emotion of the noise that you get from these cars, of the vibration. It is just another level. And I really hope that that thing will come back."

People see you as a kind of winning machine. But obviously your character is much more complex than that. Can you explain that contradiction?

"I am a winning machine when I need to be. But I can also switch off, and enjoy my life outside of racing.

"But anything racing-related, of course I am a winning machine. I demand a lot from the people in the team. They also expect me to perform and do the best job I can.

"That is what you get paid for at the end of the day. We have the same target. The same goal.

"Of course I can be very outspoken. But that is what I like. That is also with our culture.

"And that is how I approach my life also outside of F1, with my GT3 team. We do not hold back. At least for me, you need to be like that to really get the best out of everyone."

Why is speaking your mind and being honest so important to you?

"I just want to be myself. I know there are a lot of politics in Formula 1, and I understand also between the teams there are a lot of politics.

"You will always speak for yourself in terms of where you think you might have an advantage or not as a team. That is normal. Also with the engines and the chassis, it is the same thing.

"When it is good, it is good. When it is bad, it is bad. You will hear it from me because that is how I like to operate. And I am not holding back from that."

title: What drives McCoy after second big crash in 13 months?
description: After he injured his back in his second big crash in 13 months, Gary McCoy speaks to the BBC Bikes podcast about his recovery and drive to return to racing.
fullText:
When Gary McCoy slid off his bike at the Isle of Man TT in June, he had two seconds to process what was about to happen.

"'Oh no, not again.' I knew what was coming," he recalled.

The Northern Ireland road racer ended up in hospital with five broken vertebrae in his back, one of which was crushed, and a broken shoulder blade.

Just 13 months earlier, McCoy had another big crash at the North West 200 which left him with serious injuries.

On that occasion, a following rider crashed into McCoy from behind approaching Mill Road roundabout and he was left with a bleed in the brain, a punctured lung and 22 broken bones.

Yet, despite an extensive list of injuries from the two accidents, McCoy plans to get back on the bike and hit the roads again next year.

Speaking to the BBC Bikes podcast, McCoy says he was in "disbelief" after his accident at the Isle of Man TT, and says he was "very, very lucky", but the thought of competing again is not only driving on his recovery, but also his drive to get back to work.

"Whenever you want something bad enough you sort of look by it all, and it keeps you going forward," he said.

"But motorbikes is driving me on, motorbikes is driving me on to get fitter and get better, get back to work, get back to racing.

"If you didn't know motorbikes, you would have no drive. I don't think so. I don't think so. It's driving me on at the minute and long may it last."

McCoy 'awaiting results of scan on vertebrae injuries'

McCoy grew up watching road racing right across Ireland with his family, but it wasn't until he was 21 that he started competing.

He made his North West 200 debut in 2022, when he was the best newcomer, and had several top 10 finishes at the international road race.

After he recovered from his 2025 North West 200 accident, the 27-year-old was primed to make his TT debut for the family-run MadBros team in June, and things had started well.

McCoy had shown impressive form in qualifying as a newcomer but an accident in damp conditions in the opening Supersport race brought his TT debut to a sudden halt.

"Prior to the crash, everything was absolutely amazing. It was the best thing I've ever done," McCoy added.

"It's all I've ever wanted to do from when I was three or four years of age.

"So, after twenty seven years of wanting to do it, and finally getting to do it, it was unbelievable."

On his crash, which happened at the Kerrowmoar section of the 37.73-mile circuit on the third lap of the race, McCoy was still looking at the positives.

"We were just caught out in the damp patch and chatting to a few others, even Michael Dunlap said to the boys he had a wee moment down through it, and Paul Jordan had a wee moment through it.

"A few top boys were having moments, you know, so it's just unfortunate that a newcomer had to get caught out and that is what it is."

McCoy has two young children and a wife, Leana, and admits that road racing is "a very selfish sport".

He admits Leana would be happy if he stayed away from the bike and there is a lot of pressure on her, but she is supportive of him racing.

McCoy says he moved back in with his mum and dad for three months after his 2025 crash as Leana was dealing with a newborn, and says she is a "strong woman".

"You just think it is never going to be you in that situation," McCoy said about the dangers of the sport."

"All I wanted to do was race motorbikes and I'm doing it.

"I can't really explain it any more than that. It's all I've ever wanted. So I'm doing it and I'm not going to give up on it."

McCoy says his full focus is on returning to the North West 200 and Isle of Man TT, where he wants to be progressing.

For the TT in particular, the Cookstown rider said he "can't describe the feeling" of getting ready to set off down Bray Hill for the opening laps.

"Until you actually experience it and until you actually experience it and do the Isle of Man TT, you can't really explain what it means or how it feels.

Listen to the BBC Bikes podcast with Gary McCoy and Stephen Watson on BBC Sounds.

title: Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season
description: Who are favourites to reach the Super Bowl and who will be the surprise standouts? BBC's NFL experts make their predictions for the 2026 season - and so can you.
fullText:
The NFL is notoriously difficult to predict and last season was no different.

Seven of the eight division winners were different from 2024, with two of the Super Bowl favourites missing out on the play-offs entirely - the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs.

Two outsiders then made it all the way to the big game, with the Seattle Seahawks beating the New England Patriots for their first NFL championship in 12 years.

So, who will be this season's surprise package? Who will be playing at Super Bowl 61 next February? And who will be the main men?

Here, the BBC's NFL experts make their picks for the 2026 season, which begins this week. Plus you can predict your Super Bowl winner at the bottom of this page.

Rob Staton: I think the NFC will be another battle between the Los Angeles Rams and Seattle Seahawks. I'm going to go with the Rams, simply because only two teams have repeated since the turn of the century. I have them facing the Buffalo Bills. Josh Allen finally gets to the big game.

Hugh Ferris: You could argue that, aside from an underwhelming head coach hire, there's little reason the 2026 Bills will be any different to the recent incarnations. I'm picking them to finally get over the line, though, and reach the Super Bowl, but to lose nonetheless. It's incredibly difficult to choose anyone else rather than the Rams, isn't it?

Haydn Parry: Surely the Bills can convert Allen's talent and make it to the season showpiece? Joe Brady's promotion to head coach might prove to be the missing ingredient. From the NFC, I think the Rams look most likely to have a strong tilt this campaign, and I see them winning it.

Joe Bradshaw: The last time the Super Bowl was at SoFi Stadium in 2022, the Rams won on home territory and they look primed to repeat next February. From the AFC, surely Bills quarterback Allen is overdue a trip to the NFL's biggest game, even if it will ultimately end in defeat.

David Brindle: After losing Bo Nix to injury in last season's play-offs, I expect the Denver Broncos to use that as motivation and at least go one further this season. As for the Rams, it's very difficult to look past the consensus predictions for the Super Bowl.

Ben Collins: Full disclosure, I'd seen the above before writing this so here's some leftfield picks... imagine if it's the Los Angeles Chargers that actually get to play in the Super Bowl in their own stadium, and it's former Rams quarterback Jared Goff that leads Detroit to victory.

Rob Staton: I'm going with Josh Allen. He now has an offensive-minded head coach running the team. Everything will be geared towards him having a big season.

Hugh Ferris: In an attempt to think outside the box, I'm picking Justin Herbert of the Chargers. You might suggest a quarterback in a Jim Harbaugh team isn't likely to get the chance to have an MVP-level season, but the hiring of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator might change that.

Haydn Parry: I might be wearing my blue-star goggles here but Dak Prescott has the ability and the weapons to have an outstanding season. Offence was not the Dallas Cowboys' problem last year and it certainly wasn't Prescott's fault that the team failed to deliver. Dallas just need to find a 'D'.

Joe Bradshaw: Buffalo's new head coach Joe Brady has stepped up from offensive coordinator so knows how to get Josh Allen purring. If the Bills make the Super Bowl, their quarterback will be the obvious candidate for his second MVP award.

David Brindle: If it wasn't to be a quarterback, I fancy Jahmyr Gibbs. He's signed a new deal and now has no running back competition at Detroit so expect him to see lots of action on a Lions team who are NFC contenders.

Ben Collins: Cincinnati have remedied their defence and still have a top offence. After twice winning comeback player of the year, quarterback Joe Burrow stays fit long enough to bag the award he really wants as the Bengals make a deep play-off run.

Rob Staton: It could be Joe Brady if he can help Josh Allen reach MVP status, but in order to mix things up I'm going for DeMeco Ryans. The Houston Texans are going to lead on their defence and I think they'll be really strong.

Hugh Ferris: If the Bills reach the Super Bowl, then it stands to reason Joe Brady gets the nod as a first-year head coach, putting to shame people (like me) who called him an underwhelming hire.

Haydn Parry: I have always been a big fan of John Harbaugh. He will start from a comparatively low base in New York with the Giants, but with their passionate fanbase and the enormous potential of Jaxson Dart lift-off could be achieved early.

Joe Bradshaw: There has been such turnover on the NFL's coaching carousel, it has been hard to keep up this off-season. In the face of such instability, I'll opt for Sean McVay as he steers the Rams to their third Super Bowl title.

David Brindle: I'm going for Sean Payton to pick up his second award, 20 years after winning it with New Orleans. With the work done so far and decisions Payton has already made at Denver, this is the year I think it'll be formally recognised.

Ben Collins: After Detroit were hindered by a defensive injury crisis last season, Dan Campbell is rewarded as he gets the Lions roaring again.

Rob Staton: I'd expect Rueben Bain to have an immediate impact in Tampa Bay. Jadarian Price will get opportunities to shine in Seattle. I was a big fan of De'Zhaun Stribling, taken by the San Francisco 49ers. But in terms of pure impact, give me Caleb Downs, the safety in Dallas.

Hugh Ferris: The 49ers have one wide receiver AWOL, another out for the season, and injury question marks over Mike Evans and George Kittle - who's recovering from a torn Achilles - so along with a returning Deebo Samuel, there's a gap for De'Zhaun Stribling to fill.

Haydn Parry: It will be interesting to see how wide receiver Carnell Tate, fourth overall pick by Tennessee, adapts among the big boys. With his versatile skillset, the Titans expect him to contribute right from the off - the pre-draft scout reports highlighted his maturity, intelligence, sure hands and catch radius.

Joe Bradshaw: De'Zhaun Stribling was a surprise selection by the 49ers at the start of the second round but given their annual injury issues, he could be in line for plenty of work this season. Some fine displays in pre-season have only increased the hype.

David Brindle: After Kenneth Walker departed, the Seahawks picked Jadarian Price in the draft. He'll start the season as their lead back, with Zach Charbonnet still recovering from an ACL tear. I expect him to keep that job and become a top running back in the league for many years.

Ben Collins: Sonny Styles' athleticism caught the eye of NFL teams during the pre-draft process. He could have a big impact at linebacker for the Washington Commanders and soon become one of their leaders.

Rob Staton: I'm not suggesting the Las Vegas Raiders are going to go on an improbable run or anything, but Klint Kubiak did an excellent job in Seattle [as offensive coordinator] and should make the transition to head coach with ease. I think this will be the year, finally, that the Raiders show signs of growth.

Hugh Ferris: Here's a surprise: the New York teams won't both be terrible. The Jets' draft and John Harbaugh going to the Giants should mean they could rise to the heady heights of being mediocre.

Haydn Parry: Fernando Mendoza worked wonders at Indiana last year. He probably needs to perform miracles in Las Vegas but it will be fascinating to follow his progress. The lad needs broad shoulders to carry the weight of expectation but the Raiders can hardly do worse than last season.

Joe Bradshaw: Can you call a team with consecutive 11-win seasons a surprise package? Despite great regular seasons, the Los Angeles Chargers have faltered in the play-offs but they are now healthy again and new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel looks a perfect fit for talented quarterback Justin Herbert.

David Brindle: Given they missed the play-offs and went 6-11 last season, if the Cincinnati Bengals can stay healthy - especially quarterback Joe Burrow, who missed most of last season with turf toe - they could reach the Super Bowl and upset the status quo.

Ben Collins: Kevin Stefanski was twice named coach of the year at Cleveland and now has a more stable team at his disposal in Atlanta, led by dual-threat running back Bijan Robinson. If the Falcons can settle on a quarterback, they could finally get back in play-off contention.

Rob Staton: The Cleveland Browns are a shambles. The situation surrounding Deshaun Watson is a mess, and it's frankly incredible he's still in the league. They can no longer rely on Myles Garrett. They seem destined to fail.

Hugh Ferris: I picked the Browns last year and got it wrong. That won't stop me doing it again this year. They're going with Deshaun Watson as their starting quarterback, which will do little other than prove one more time that it might have been the worst trade (and contract) in NFL history.

Haydn Parry: There seems to be a general consensus that the Miami Dolphins are 'in transition' - which is NFL-speak for 'total rebuild'. They are probably in a race to the bottom with the Arizona Cardinals as things stand.

Joe Bradshaw: Iconic edge rusher Myles Garrett has left the Browns and they still have huge questions at quarterback with Deshaun Watson booed by his own fans during pre-season. Their best hope is a top pick in 2027's stacked-looking draft.

David Brindle: Until now, all of the questions have been tough, but this is easy. After a tumultuous off-season where they moved on from Jaylen Waddle and others, the rebuild is under way for the Miami Dolphins and they face a daunting season.

Ben Collins: Although I'm rooting for British tight end Seydou Traore in his rookie year, this could be a long season for the Dolphins. Their roster looks short on talent having also let Tua Tagovailoa and Tyreek Hill go, with Malik Willis entering a season as starting quarterback for the first time.

title: Russell hindered or just Antonelli brilliance? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Italian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli climbed from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix - his home race - in one of the great Formula 1 drives.

Antonelli extended his lead at the top of the drivers' standings to 66 points over team-mate George Russell.

Max Verstappen, in the Red Bull, finished third to complete the podium at Monza.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 14 of the 2026 season in Madrid, Spain.

Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore

Why wasn't George Russell given the opportunity by Mercedes to pit under the virtual safety car in the Italian Grand Prix? I know he had the hard tyres on, but as the lead driver on track should he not have been at least given the choice? - Tom

In hindsight, it would be easy to think there would be some controversy around the decisions that were taken when the virtual safety car was called mid-race at the Italian Grand Prix.

In reality, though, there was not any.

At the time, George Russell was leading the race on the hard tyre and Kimi Antonelli was second on the medium, a few laps after the Mercedes drivers had been advised to call off their 'yo-yo' scrapping to allow them to optimise their pace and build a gap to Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

Without a VSC, the question was whether the mediums on Antonelli's car would last to the end - probably not - and what Mercedes would do about that.

With or without the VSC, the race result was up in the air.

The VSC changed the complexion of the race, but Russell, who had fitted hards at the red flag with the express intention of going to the end, said he had given no thought to changing tyres at the time.

"I didn't," he said. "I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well. But I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pit wall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.

"And of course, when we had Max in the mix as well, from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios.

"If either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre. But it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive."

At the time, Mercedes' strategy computers were saying staying out was the best option.

Team principal Toto Wolff said: "We didn't know what was the better strategy. At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."

All of which goes to underline the main takeaway - the sublime quality of Antonelli's drive.

He made remarkable progress up through the field from 19th on the grid, wasting no time in picking off cars in front, minimising any loss from overtaking to his overall race time.

He made this look easy, but as many other drivers proved at Monza on Sunday, overtaking another car of similar performance and immediately pulling away was anything but.

This was a performance for the ages - like Lewis Hamilton in Brazil in 2021, Max Verstappen in Brazil in 2024 or 2025, or Fernando Alonso in Valencia in 2012.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, who knows a thing or two about this sort of performance having worked with Michael Schumacher and Alonso, said: "While he had a very competitive car, we have to say that he beat a team-mate starting second on the grid.

"It's a very special day, very important for his championship. But for his career and for the fans, motorsport in general, this will be an iconic day. This will be remembered in the years to come."

Is Charles Leclerc's tendency to crash out of races starting to become a problem both for him and Ferrari? - Nathan

Charles Leclerc certainly did not have his best day in Monza on Sunday.

He was arguably too aggressive with Lewis Hamilton at the first chicane on the first lap, forcing his team-mate into the gravel and dropping him to 10th, and crashed out a lap later.

"I wouldn't say that this is the issue," he said. "From lap one to lap two, I had a bit of a difference in power delivery. We'll look into it, but I don't want to comment too much before checking the data and confirming it 100%."

Having said that, does the allegation that Leclerc has a "tendency to crash out of races" stand up?

He has done it twice so far this year - the previous time was in Monaco, when he lost control at a restart on the broken track surface at Anthony Noghes.

But, unless I've missed something, you have to go back nearly three years to the one before that, when he retired with car damage after an incident-packed race at Zandvoort in 2023.

In that period, for comparison, Hamilton has done the same thing four times - Brazil and Netherlands last year, Austin in 2024 and Qatar in 2023.

Ferrari clearly have some things to sort out, however, in terms of their operations and general approach.

Hamilton is not happy about the way the team have effectively disregarded his - albeit slim - title hopes this year in favour of driver equality, and he said after dropping more points to Antonelli on Sunday that it was "far too late for those decisions to come".

The incident between Leclerc and Hamilton on lap one took place in the context of Hamilton saying after qualifying they had to "work as a team to try and topple" Mercedes.

Leclerc said of the first-corner incident: "I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other. I mean, honestly, Zandvoort there was way too many talks already.

"Here it's true, though, that we went too far. Lewis in Turn One, then Turn Two, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough and doing it here is not good."

Hamilton was not impressed by the suggestion he had done anything wrong at Turn One.

When those remarks were put to Hamilton, he said: "He said what? I was ahead in Turn Two. By the ethics, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it."

He added: "I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space."

Team boss Frederic Vasseur, who said he would talk to the drivers before discussing this in the media, has some smoothing out to do before this weekend's race in Madrid.

Listen - Italian GP Review: History at Monza!

Aston Martin have had their major upgrades but were right at the back of the grid again in Monza. Have the upgrades just failed? - Colin

Aston Martin had a major car upgrade in Hungary two races ago, and a "spec two" Honda engine at the race before Italy in Zandvoort, on either side of the summer break.

There is no question the car upgrade worked. What was effectively an all-new car, apart from the rear suspension and gearbox, cut lap times by about two seconds.

Fernando Alonso made it into the second part of qualifying for the first time all year in Hungary, and drove an outstanding race to finish ninth on merit in the Netherlands, on a one-stop strategy, holding at arm's length the faster Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Racing Bull of Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

More upgrades are expected, in the form of a weight reduction around the gearbox, for either Madrid this weekend or Azerbaijan.

The Honda engine upgrade that made its debut in Zandvoort has been less impressive, which is why Aston Martin found themselves at the back again on the power-sensitive Monza track.

Trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara says Honda "observed a step forward in terms of performance from our metrics".

But if there has been one, it is small. Drivability of the spec two in Zandvoort was noticeably worse, too, although it had made a step forward in Italy.

The Aston Martin car seems to be a midfield-level chassis now, somewhere around the borderline of getting into the final part of qualifying, depending on circuit layout, if it had a competitive engine.

And on the chassis side, the team have a sense of direction that gives them confidence they can make another step next season.

With Honda, which still has comfortably the worst engine in F1, the upgrade has been less reassuring.

What is the new Madring circuit in Spain like in terms of power compared to all the previously visited circuits? Who is it expected to suit most of all? - Andrew

The Madrid circuit which makes its debut this weekend has been built from scratch.

The circuit layout has lots of corners, and it is expected to have a low power sensitivity, around the level of Zandvoort.

Medium-speed corners predominate. And overtaking is expected to be difficult - again, like Zandvoort, or even Hungary.

Given Lando Norris took dominant wins in the Netherlands and Hungary, some teams believe McLaren might be favourites heading into this weekend, but McLaren themselves are not so sure.

Hungary and Zandvoort have long-duration corners, where the McLaren excels. But the Madring corners are generally short duration, the exception being the long, banked Monumental, which is expected to be flat out.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said after the race in Monza on Sunday: "We still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.

"Yet, we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary we were in position to win races and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race.

"Drag will be less important in Madrid. There is a much higher density of corners. We will definitely give it a go."

New tracks always throw up surprises. So, in short, while one can speculate about car and circuit characteristics all one wants, no one will actually know until qualifying on Saturday.

title: Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms
description:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’
The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.
In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.

It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.

The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.

Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.

In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.

“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.

“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”

The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”

Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.

Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.

The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.

Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.

Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.

Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.

“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”

Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.

However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

title: Self-described 'genocidal racist monster' jailed after BBC investigation
description: A former tax worker is sentenced to two years for inciting hatred online.
fullText:
Thomas Webster was investigated by police after comments he made to an undercover journalist in a BBC programme

Warning: This article contains graphic accounts of racist and violent language

A former tax worker who described himself as "the ultimate genocidal racist monster" has been jailed for inciting hatred online after he was exposed by a BBC investigation.

Thomas Webster was sacked by HMRC and investigated by police after comments he made to an undercover journalist in the BBC programme 'Unmasked: Extreme Far Right'.

Webster, 29, from Lapworth, Warwickshire, admitted 10 counts of stirring up racial hatred online, including ones calling for the killing and extinction of his racial "enemies".

Webster also admitted to stirring up religious hatred and another count of stirring up hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation. He was sentenced to two years at Warwick Crown Court.

In his online posts, Webster said he wanted Jewish and gay people to be tortured and executed.

Webster also said he wanted to kill all Muslims until they were "globally extinct."

In one instance, he said if a migrant hotel was placed on his road he would "prepare for murder and prison time, I am serious".

Webster was a member of the far right group Patriotic Alternative when BBC Wales Investigates' undercover reporter secretly recorded him at two of the group's events in 2024.

He was filmed saying that in his job at HMRC he liked to "deliberately" give non-white people "bad information which sounds interesting, like I'm deliberately trying to sabotage them."

Webster was dismissed by HMRC in February 2025, a month after the programme was broadcast.

The HMRC said it took breaches of its standards "extremely seriously" and had "robust processes" in place to investigate concerns.

"Where standards are not met, we act decisively," HMRC said in a statement.

"Following an internal disciplinary process, the individual concerned was dismissed from HMRC and ceased to be employed by the department in February 2025."

Talking to an undercover BBC reporter, Webster self-identified as a "white totalitarianist" who believed in "a world where white becomes the default human race... all other races will be extinct."

Describing himself as "a guy who seeks trouble" while on a hike with other Patriotic Alternative members, he boasted that he would have "crushed [the] skulls" of a group of non-white men if they had walked near to him.

Following the BBC programme, police opened an investigation and linked Webster to several social media accounts, mainly on X.

He was arrested for inciting racial hatred in September 2025 and police used details on his phone and computer to confirm the accounts were his. He was charged in July and pleaded guilty last month.

A number of the offending posts were still visible on X in the weeks after Webster pleaded guilty, as well as dozens of others in which he used the most extreme racist language.

In these additional posts, which did not form part of the charges, Webster praised Adolf Hitler and the Nazis and told several prominent politicians that they should be killed or subjected to sexual violence.

In one of his X posts, Webster described himself as a "genocidal racist monster."

He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"

After BBC contacted X about the posts, they were taken down - but the company did not comment further.

Days before Webster's sentencing, BBC News found another active Substack account appearing to belong to him.

The account shared posts discussing Webster's arrest, as well as intimate details of his personal life.

It also included several comments about race, including one calling for the "total genetic extinction" of people from South Asia.

One comment claimed that these posts were made in spite of bail conditions heavily limiting Webster's internet use and explicitly preventing him from communicating via social media.

After the BBC contacted Substack about the content, most of the posts were taken down, although one for which Webster was charged is still visible. The company did not respond further.

Warwick Crown Court heard Webster had been referred four times to the UK Government-led Prevent programme, a scheme aimed to stop people becoming terrorists.

The court also heard police found a crossbow in the attic of his property, which was still in its wrapping.

Jamie Scott, prosecuting, told the court that the CPS took a "proportionate approach" to charging him with 12 offences - but asked it be noted that there was "a raft" of similar material posted online by Webster.

His defence lawyer Susan Guest said Webster had a long-standing difficulty around social interaction and anxiety and said he became "more isolated" where his views were "reinforced rather than challenged" by people online.

"He almost lived in a bubble and this online community reinforced his views," Guest told the court.

"That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."

Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour.

"Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views.

"I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't sent you to custody."

Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech."

"Expressing a wish for people to be killed… Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as well… and encouraging other people to express similar views.

"It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.

Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again.

"Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.

Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

title: England v Australia significant opportunity for six-caps Burns
description: As Delaney Burns hopes to be selected to face Australia, she talks to BBC Sport about another opportunity to add to her six caps in a so-far whirlwind career.
fullText:
Delaney Burns revealed to her England team-mates that at 15 years old she had a 'short back and sides' - it went down well.

Having been selected to speak at one of the Red Roses 'connection meetings', the 24-year-old admitted she had "never been so nervous to talk in front of a group of people" in her life.

But the second-row was a roaring success as she covered her rugby journey, life in Bristol and 'that' haircut.

As she prepares to face Australia this Saturday, she has another opportunity to add to her six caps in what has been a whirlwind career so far.

Still only 24, Burns won her first three caps for England in 2023, then had to patiently wait for a call-up into the 2026 Six Nations squad to add three more.

With Abbie Ward, Rosie Galligan and Zoe Stratford all away from the squad pregnant or on maternity leave, the upcoming WXV Global Series is a significant opportunity for Burns.

"This is the first kind of campaign that I've been brought in from the start," she says.

"Being deemed as a more experienced forward, especially around the line-out, is something I want to hold myself quite high to and we do have a few younger players in the squad now, a few people coming through. So, I'm just trying to be a bit more of a person of knowledge to look to and help them out and build on my own strength."

Having missed out on one of England's 32-contracted places, she's focusing on her defence this season and wants to reach the next level.

As Burns continues to find her feet in the squad, an area she's excelled in off-field has been her work with the Bristol Bears Foundation. She coaches and gives talks to girls at schools in the greater Bristol area, covering more than just rugby.

"We talk about the menstrual cycle and how it affects you," she says. "Rugby is a really good sport to help with the idea of body image.

"We look at the effects that social media has in terms of too much screen time and filtering and AI. How to stay mentally safe as well as physically safe.

"There's some really deprived areas of Bristol - our whole mantra is to take those areas and do what we can to give the kids in those communities an opportunity, which I find very rewarding."

The impact of the work she's done with the foundation has seen the launch of a South Bristol girls team that's attracted 50-60 players and counting.

As she seeks a seventh cap against Australia on Saturday, will she take any of her own advice?

"I should listen to my own voice a bit more, probably," she says. "There are times where I definitely find myself in a bit of a weird headspace, camp is always hard.

"It's really rewarding and it's an exciting place to be and I wouldn't change it for the world, but equally it can be quite difficult. So yeah, listening to my own advice probably would be quite beneficial."

One of Burns' greatest fans is her grandad. If selected on Saturday, he'll be making the trip up to Manchester from Poole.

"He got me into rugby, trained me and goes to all the games he can," she says.

The stories about old hairstyles may have raised a few smiles among team-mates, but Burns is taking a more serious approach to the season ahead.

If selected against Australia, she will have another opportunity to add to her international experience and strengthen her place in an increasingly competitive Red Roses squad, with one of her biggest supporters watching on from the stands.

title: Champions League returns - who are favourites and players to watch?
description: The Champions League is back and BBC Sport take a look at who the favourites are to win the title plus predictions from the experts.
fullText:
The Champions League is back - who will get their hands on the famous trophy in Madrid on 5 June next year?

Paris St-Germain are aim to win the title for the third year running as the league phase begins on Tuesday.

Five English teams will try to stop them with Arsenal the favourites to better their runners-up slot from last year.

We asked football experts Julien Laurens and Guillem Balague who they think will win the tournament and took a look at what the statistics said. And you can vote for who you think will be crowned champions below.

Don't forget the BBC will again show highlights of the Champions League this season.

From 22:00 BST on the Wednesday of Champions League weeks, there will be match-by-match highlights available on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, plus a special Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One at 22:40.

This week there will also be be a highlights show on Thursday on BBC Two at 22:30 with highlights from Thursday's matches dropping at 22:00.

If PSG do the three-peat, it would be an incredible achievement. I don't think they will do it. I think two in a row is already special - three in a row is impossible unless you've got Cristiano Ronaldo in your team, which they don't.

I think they will be close. I think they'll reach at least the semi-final, but I think going for three in a row is tough.

I don't believe fully in the Jose Mourinho-Real Madrid project, so I would go for Bayern Munich and Arsenal to reach the final. They are probably the teams, other than PSG, who have deserved to be there the most in the past two seasons. To win it, I'll go for Arsenal. They have the best defence in Europe by far and that's what wins you titles. I would go for PSG to reach the last four, Bayern close runners-up and Arsenal to win it.

With PSG's irregular start to the season we are seeing how difficult it is to maintain the level. Luis Enrique continues to push the team to be in the vanguard of football which is demanding, with dynamic football and relentless pressure. With the league phase considered a place to experiment and prepare for the second half of the season, there will be a time of transition and strange results before the crunch time in January onwards.

As the main axis is there, I expect them to get very close to winning it again.

But Barcelona are flying. They would like another centre-back and a number nine. It is what Hansi Flick wanted to get to the next level but he feels they are on the way to the top anyway.

Arsenal have found a way to win regularly, and with that off their shoulders, players feel a release that will make them play better. Those three should be in the semis unless they meet before. The fourth, again draw permitting, should be Bayern Munich, Real Madrid or Manchester City.

I have picked five players to watch in this year's Champions League. The first is Jude Bellingham. This is a very big season for him individually and collectively for Real Madrid under Mourinho in the number 10 role that I think suits him well. After a very good World Cup, I think that momentum will carry. I expect him to score a lot of goals and to be very strong and be decisive.

Como's number 10 Nico Paz is at the heart of everything they do with the ball. It's their first time in the Champions League. Cesc Fabregas is the manager, so they're a very entertaining team, nice to watch. Paz is a special player - very much in the making - but he will be a top player very soon.

Mr Champions League - Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. In the past two seasons, he's been incredible at PSG, especially last year on that left wing where he can cut inside or go on the outside, he's a threat with the right foot and the left foot, he scored some great goals, he's really good technically. I think he's in the running for the Ballon d'Or. He's one of those players that gets you on the edge of your sofa. He's the guy.

Lens are back in the Champions League having pushed PSG all the way last year in Ligue 1 - and Ismaelo Ganiou is arguably their best player. A strong centre-back, 21 years old, good on the ball, very quick and physical. I expect him to leave at the end of the season for a big Premier League club.

Since leaving Aston Villa to go to Roma, Donyell Malen has been incredible, scoring almost a goal per game as a lone striker for Gian Piero Gasperini's side. Roma being back in the Champions League is great and they're a very entertaining team to watch again. I think we will see Malen back to his best level.

Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane is in a campaign to win the Ballon d'Or. He deserves to be in contention and I do not expect him to drop his level as Bayern's style suits him greatly.

Teenager Lamine Yamal is hungry for more and has set his sights on the Champions League. Hansi Flick wants a team that defends high and passionately so he can shine.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia has got another level and with PSG going far he will again rescue the team and win big games. He will be a Ballon d'Or winner soon.

Shakhtar have a long tradition of converting Brazilian stars into European multimillion transfers and 20-year-old Kaua Elias could be the next one on the list.

After a difficult season for Martin Odegaard last year with injuries, he has started this one very well. The Norwegian can dominate games, and his team - more confident now - will need him to do that. He seems ready to take that leadership.

According to Opta, last year's runners-up Arsenal are the overall favourites to win the Champions League (20.4%) although Bayern Munich, who lost to PSG in the semi-finals, are only marginally behind (20%).

PSG's chances of winning a third European title in a row are 7.3%, fourth overall, while 2023 winners Manchester City are third, having been given a 12.7% chance.

All five of the Premier League teams are ranked inside the top 10 for overall win probability and all have been given a more than 50% chance of reaching the last-16.

When it comes to the league phase, Liverpool have the easiest draw according to Opta's power rankings while Stuttgart have the easiest run overall and Inter Milan the most favourable of the teams from pot one.

Arsenal also have a relatively favourable draw. Despite drawing Real Madrid and Bayern Munich from pot one, Mikel Arteta's side also drew the two lowest-ranked sides in the competition - Sabah and Slovan Bratislava.

Manchester City face the toughest fixtures of the English clubs with only five teams receiving a tougher draw overall. They have drawn two European giants from pot one in Barcelona and PSG, while 24th-ranked Napoli are a particularly difficult test from pot three.

Last season, Arsenal finished top of the league phase after being given one of the easiest fixture lists according to Opta, while Bayern Munich finished second despite being handed the toughest set of opponents of all 36 sides.

I love what Fabregas is doing with Como and the fact he has decided to stay despite receiving interesting offers in the past two years. He can get it wrong and nothing will happen, which gives the freedom to keep developing his ideas. He has swum against the tide and now he is very much in the train of modern football, and at the front. I expect them to reach the knock-out stages.

In getting past Celtic, Austrian outfit LASK showed a big competitive level. A home win somewhere and a respectable points tally would be a fair result for their first campaign. But they probably will not qualify.

Azerbaijan side Sabah are very interesting - a success based on organisation - but trips to Arsenal and Manchester United and home games against Barcelona and Borussia Dortmund is a tough introduction. They will give us one or two surprising results, but not enough to go through.

Viking face Bayern, Atletico, Napoli and Aston Villa, but Norwegian football is full of clever, competitive coaches, players and teams. They could make it to the knock-outs.

title: Trump set to attend star-studded Irish Open at Doonbeg
description: BBC Sport looks ahead to the Irish Open with Rory McIlroy trying to defend the title and President Trump poised to attend.
fullText:
With the dust settling on Great Britain and Ireland's dramatic Walker Cup win at Lahinch, the action shifts 16 miles further down the west coast of Ireland as a quality field descends on Doonbeg for the 2026 Irish Open.

Twelve months ago, The K Club staged an Irish Open for the ages as home favourite Rory McIlroy captured his second title in dramatic fashion.

The six-time major winner again headlines a stellar field as Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in County Clare hosts the tournament for the first time.

The Irish Open precedes the tour's flagship event, the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, which will be played next week.

With several star names in action and no shortage of storylines to follow throughout the week, here is everything you need to know about the Irish Open.

A lot. Five months after completing the career Grand Slam with a memorable win at the Masters, McIlroy sealed an emotional win in front of an ecstatic Irish crowd by beating Joakim Lagergren in a play-off.

Trailing Lagergren by two shots on the 72nd hole, McIlroy sunk a 25-foot eagle putt to take the Swede to a play-off and eventually prevailed on the third extra hole.

It was a gripping final round as McIlroy tussled for the trophy with Lagergren, overnight leader Adrien Saddier, Angel Hidalgo and Rafael Cabrera-Bello, who catapulted into contention with an ace at the third.

The win - which came nine years after his first Irish Open title - provided a well-timed boost for McIlroy just three weeks before he helped Europe retain the Ryder Cup with victory over the United States at Bethpage Black in New York.

While McIlroy will attract much of the attention in Doonbeg, he must fend off a high-quality field if he is to join European legends Seve Ballesteros, Nick Faldo, Bernhard Langer and Colin Montgomerie on three Irish Open wins.

As always, there is a strong Irish contingent. Shane Lowry, who memorably won his national title as an amateur in 2009, is chasing his first individual win in four years. The 2019 Open champion finished tied 15th last year.

Tom McKibbin arrives in decent form. The 23-year-old was in contention for last month's British Masters before a triple bogey early in the final round meant he had to settle for tied sixth.

Three-time major champion Padraig Harrington and two-time PGA Tour winner Seamus Power add further Irish interest.

Beyond the home hopes, there are a host of notable names. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm joins McIlroy in chasing a third Irish Open win after successes at Portstewart in 2017 and Lahinch two years later.

The Spaniard tees it up in Ireland amid ongoing uncertainty around LIV Golf's future. The breakaway tour, which launched in 2022, ended its season early following the withdrawal of the Public Investment Fund's financial backing.

McKibbin, England's Tyrrell Hatton and Chile's Joaquin Niemann are among the other LIV players in Ireland this week.

In addition, there is a strong European Ryder Cup flavour in the form of captain Luke Donald, Robert MacIntyre, Sepp Straka and twins Nicolai and Rasmus Hojgaard, who pipped McIlroy to the 2024 Irish Open at Royal County Down.

Five-time major winner Brooks Koepka also returns after missing the cut on his Irish Open debut last year.

US President Donald Trump - who owns the Doonbeg venue - is expected to attend the Irish Open.

Trump will be in Ireland this week as part of a two-day visit during which he will meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and hold a bilateral meeting with the Taoiseach [Irish prime minister] Micheal Martin.

He is expected to arrive in Ireland on Saturday and may present the Irish Open winner with the trophy on Sunday evening.

Donald Trump to meet Irish president on two day visit

The tee times will be released on Tuesday.

The Irish Open was first staged in 1927 and this week is the 71st edition of the event.

The tournament has been played at 21 courses across the island of Ireland, including renowned links venues Royal Portrush, Royal County Down and Portmarnock, which has hosted the tournament a record 19 times.

The cream of European talent competed during the 1980s and 1990s particularly.

Former winners include McIlroy, Rahm, Padraig Harrington, Sergio Garcia, Jose Maria Olazabal, Montgomerie, Faldo, Ian Woosnam, Ballesteros, Sam Torrance and Ben Crenshaw.

Formerly known simply as Doonbeg, the links course was designed by former world number one Greg Norman and opened in 2002.

It was redesigned by architect Martin Hawtree before the property was acquired by Trump in 2014 and renamed.

Unusually for a tour course, the layout boasts five par-fives and five par-threes. The signature hole is the par-three 14th, which can play as short as 111 yards.

fullText:
Round 14 of the 2026 Formula 1 season heads to the new Madring circuit, for the Spanish Grand Prix, from 11-13 September.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli came back from 19th on the grid for a spectacular win in front of his home fans at the Italian Grand Prix.

In another surprise during the weekend, Alpine's Pierre Gasly managed to secure the first pole position of his career on Saturday.

Antonelli was joined by his Mercedes team-mate George Russell on the Monza podium, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen third.

It was a disappointing weekend for Ferrari, with Charles Leclerc crashing out of the race and Lewis Hamilton finishing sixth.

Lights out for Sunday's 57-lap race will be at 14:00 BST.

Commentary of the race will be available across BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra 2, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

You can also listen by asking most smart speakers to "play Sports Extra 2".

Make sure to listen to every episode of the Chequered Flag podcast. For the first time this year, the post-race show for every grand prix is available to watch on BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

The Madring has replaced the Barcelona-Catalunya circuit as the home of the Spanish Grand Prix.

The new purpose-built track, which will run for 5.47km around 20 corners, incorporates both street-circuit and road-course sections around the Ifema Exhibition Centre between the Spanish capital and Barajas airport.
